defense_name: UNNAMED: secure prompt strategies for robotic navigation
source_title: A Study on Prompt Injection Attack Against LLM-Integrated Mobile Robotic Systems
baselines_compared: Only an internal no-defence control of the same GPT-4o robot system at matched attack rates. No competing defense and no competing attack method is compared, although the related-work section discusses Navigational Prompt Engineering (Wen et al.) without evaluating it.
key_result: Secure prompting with a reasoning-first response format yields a headline 30.8% general improvement (overall attack detection improvement plus 24.4% overall performance improvement). The sharpest finding is that Goal Hijacking Injection is completely undetectable without the defense (precision, recall and F1 all exactly zero), while with the defense precision rises to 0.9-1.0 but recall reaches only 0.13-0.54; mission performance (MOER) under OMI attack recovers from a 0.5-to-0.13 decline to a peak of 0.67. Costs are a 23.9% weighted response-time increase and 2.9% more tokens.
technical_summary: Evaluates prompt injection against a GPT-4o-controlled mobile robot whose navigation decisions come directly from multi-modal sensory prompts. Defines two injection classes the authors name Obvious Malicious Injection, which contradicts common sense, and Goal Hijacking Injection, which reads as a plausible navigation instruction while contradicting the mission objective, plus a control-signal variant the LLM cannot identify at all. Applies a secure prompting mitigation that forces the LLM to reason over each modality in natural language and then emit a per-modality attack verdict in a structured response format. Measures detection precision/recall/F1 and a mission-oriented efficiency rate across sweeping attack rates in the EyeSim VR simulator, reporting a 30.8% aggregate improvement under a bespoke weighted metric.
datasets_benchmarks: None - no public benchmark. The authors run their own simulated mission-oriented navigation scenarios in EyeSim VR with multi-modal input (camera image, LiDAR scan, human instruction), sweeping injected-attack rates of 0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 1.0.

baselines_compared: Three feature-attribution localizers adapted to this task - Single Feature Attribution (SFA), Feature Removal Attribution (FRA) and Shapley Value Attribution (SVA) - each also in a threshold-tuned variant (SFA-T, FRA-T, SVA-T) using the same validation set. A concurrent segment-classification method and Abdelnabi et al.'s distance-to-primary detector are additionally adapted for localization and compared. Baselines are inapplicable on AgentDojo because they need full output probabilities, which GPT-4o does not expose.
key_result: PromptLocate reaches 0.93-0.99 localization (RL) and ES scores with 0.95-1.00 precision and recall across all attack settings on OpenPromptInjection, and above 0.95 on AgentDojo Banking and above 0.85 on Travel and Workspace, with attack success after removal dropping sharply even where recall is lower. The striking robustness result is that its DataSentinel-based oracle still misses 63% of contaminated segments at segment level (81% untailored), yet the segment-group search and contextual-inconsistency step recover accurate localization anyway. Two competing approaches score only 0.53/0.53 and 0.76/0.72 RL/ES on the same Combined Attack; runtime is about 11 seconds per contaminated sample on an RTX A5000.
technical_summary: Proposes PromptLocate, the first method for localizing an injected prompt inside contaminated data rather than merely detecting that contamination occurred, motivated by post-attack forensics and clean-data recovery. Splits contaminated data into semantically coherent segments using a threshold tuned on a validation set, then identifies instruction-contaminated segments with a segment-group-based search over a detector repurposed as an oracle, and finally pinpoints data-contaminated segments via contextual inconsistency without needing the oracle. Evaluates across eight existing and eight adaptive attacks on OpenPromptInjection and AgentDojo, plus TaskTracker and JailbreakBench transfers. Shows the method tolerates a substantially unreliable oracle and that removing the localized span neutralizes the attack.
datasets_benchmarks: OpenPromptInjection (seven target tasks, results averaged over all 7x7 target-injected task combinations); AgentDojo (Banking, Travel, Workspace, Slack environments, injections embedded in tool-call output); TaskTracker (1,000 training / 500 test samples); JailbreakBench (100 prompts per attack type inserted into 100 clean samples); a 556-sample validation set the authors construct for threshold selection

baselines_compared: A no-preemptive-answer control ('N') for every model/dataset/CoT cell, plus cross-comparison of Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot CoT and with/without Self-Consistency. The two mitigations are compared against the unmitigated attacked condition. BadChain is discussed as a stronger dedicated attack but is not run.
key_result: Committing to an answer before reasoning measurably degrades CoT accuracy across nearly all dataset/model/CoT combinations: on GSM8K with ChatGPT, accuracy falls from 74.4 to 63.0 (unintentional) and 68.2 (malicious) under Zero-Shot CoT, and from 76.8 to 57.3 and 71.1 under Few-Shot CoT. Notably the unintentional variant is as harmful as the malicious one on the three arithmetic datasets, GPT-4 is more robust than ChatGPT, few-shot ICL provides no protection over zero-shot, and self-consistency helps but does not eliminate the loss. The two mitigations consistently lower ASR and raise accuracy but never fully negate the effect.
technical_summary: Introduces the preemptive answer scenario, in which an LLM produces an answer before it reasons, and shows that the subsequent chain-of-thought degrades to rationalizing that answer rather than deriving one. Distinguishes an unintentional variant arising from ordinary answer-first prompt phrasing from a malicious variant induced by prompt injection, and measures both with accuracy and an attack success rate across six reasoning datasets, two models and three CoT methods. Finds the incidental and adversarial variants inflict comparable damage on arithmetic tasks, which makes this one of the few papers in the corpus to instrument both failure modes under one protocol. Proposes two lightweight mitigations, problem restatement and self-reflection, which reduce but do not remove the degradation.
datasets_benchmarks: Six reasoning datasets, 500 randomly sampled test items each: GSM8K, MathQA, MATH, HotpotQA, CommonsenseQA and StrategyQA. Three CoT regimes are crossed with these: Zero-Shot CoT, Few-Shot CoT and each with Self-Consistency.

source_title: FATH: Authentication-based Test-time Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
baselines_compared: Four established test-time defenses: Instructional Prevention, Sandwich Prevention, Text Instruction Isolation (all Liu et al. 2023b) and In-context Learning Defense (Yi et al. 2023), plus a No Defense control. Attacks compared are Naive, Escape Characters, Context Ignoring, Fake Completion and Combined under Threat Model 1, plus per-defense hand-designed Adaptive Attacks under Threat Model 2.
key_result: FATH reaches the lowest ASR of any compared defense on all five Threat Model 1 attacks across three injection tasks and both backbones, driving ASR to near 0% and to exactly 0% against the Combined Attack on InjecAgent. Under Threat Model 2 adaptive attacks, which know the defense in full and are strong enough to beat Combined Attack against every other method, FATH still holds 0% ASR on GPT-3.5 and 0% on InjecAgent, with a reduced but non-zero ASR on Llama3. The cost is a small drop in judge score on benign utility.
technical_summary: Proposes FATH, a test-time defense that treats instruction handling as an authentication problem rather than a filtering problem. Generates five HMAC-derived hash tags per request, formats the prompt so user instructions and external text are segregated under input authentication tags, and prompts the LLM with a security policy requiring it to emit each response wrapped in an authorized or unauthorized output tag, aided by chain-of-thought and in-context examples. Enforces the decision outside the model by rule-based parsing of the raw output, extracting only the section carrying the correct unguessable tag, so any response elicited by an injected instruction is discarded. Evaluates on OpenPromptInjection+ and InjecAgent against four prompt-level baseline defenses under both defense-unaware and fully defense-aware adaptive attackers.
datasets_benchmarks: OpenPromptInjection+ , the authors' extension of OpenPromptInjection that swaps the 7 fixed tasks for 100 general Stanford Alpaca instructions per injection task across three injection categories (URL, QA, CLF); and InjecAgent, using all 510 direct-harm text examples

source_title: Defense against Prompt Injection Attacks via Mixture of Encodings
baselines_compared: No Defense, Datamark, Ignoring, Base64, Caesar (Hines et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2024b).
key_result: Mixture of encodings (encoding external text under Base64, Caesar and plain in parallel and aggregating the three LLM responses) matches or beats Base64/Caesar alone on attack success rate across all four BIPIA-derived safety datasets for GPT-4 and GPT-4o, while on the helpfulness benchmark it substantially outperforms Base64 and Caesar on math-heavy tasks like MMLU and MGSM and reaches performance close to the no-defense model, avoiding Base64's known utility collapse.
technical_summary: Proposes mixture of encodings, a prevention-based defense against prompt injection that encodes external text under multiple character encodings (plain, Base64, Caesar cipher) and queries the LLM once per encoding, then aggregates the responses via summed classification probabilities or an LLM meta-prompt for generation tasks. Evaluates on a BIPIA-derived safety benchmark (Email/Table/Abstract/Code) and a 9-task helpfulness benchmark against GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Shows the method keeps the low attack-success-rate of character-encoding defenses like Base64 while avoiding Base64's sharp utility loss on mathematical QA tasks such as MMLU and MGSM.
datasets_benchmarks: Safety: BIPIA-derived subset across Email (OpenAI Evals), Table (WikiTableQA), Abstract (XSum) and Code (Stack Overflow), 50 attack types. Helpfulness: 9 NLP datasets - MMLU, Squad, Hellaswag, MGSM, SamSum, WMT, IMDB, WildGuard, WebQ.

source_title: ASIDE: Architectural Separation of Instructions and Data in Language Models
baselines_compared: Vanilla (standard single-embedding architecture) and ISE (Wu et al. 2024, learnable role-offset embeddings).
key_result: Instruction-tuning with ASIDE's fixed 90-degree data-token rotation lowers indirect-injection ASR versus a Vanilla delimiter-based baseline: BIPIA-text 14.7%->4.9%, BIPIA-code 15.3%->8.8%, StruQ-ID 45.6%->28.1%, StruQ-OOD 45%->36% (averages across models), while a competing architectural method (ISE) is within 0.1-2% of Vanilla on the same benchmarks and gives essentially no improvement. Gains come with matched utility and without any dedicated safety training or adversarial examples.
technical_summary: Proposes ASIDE, a parameter-free architectural change that applies a fixed orthogonal rotation to the token embeddings of data tokens (while leaving instruction-token embeddings unchanged), giving the model an explicit, learnable-free signal of each token's functional role from the first layer onward. Requires only a modified forward pass plus standard instruction-tuning, with no retraining from scratch and no additional parameters. Evaluated across Llama 3.1/2, Qwen 3/2.5 and Mistral against a Vanilla baseline and the ISE architecture, showing markedly higher instruction-data separation (SEP score) at matched utility and consistently lower attack success rate on both direct (TensorTrust, Gandalf, Purple, RuLES) and indirect (BIPIA, StruQ) prompt-injection benchmarks, without any dedicated safety fine-tuning.
datasets_benchmarks: SEP dataset (9,160 instruction/input pairs, Zverev et al. 2025) for separation scoring; AlpacaEval 1.0 for utility; TensorTrust, Gandalf, Purple, RuLES for direct-attack ASR; BIPIA-text, BIPIA-code, StruQ-ID, StruQ-OOD for indirect-attack ASR.

source_title: UniGuardian: A Unified Defense for Detecting Prompt Injection, Backdoor Attacks and Adversarial Attacks in Large Language Models
baselines_compared: Prompt-Guard-86M; PPL Detection; Llama-Guard-3-1B; Llama-Guard-3-8B; Granite-Guardian-3.1-8B; LLM-based detection; OpenAI Moderation.
key_result: Across prompt injection, fine-tuned backdoor, and adversarial-attack settings, only UniGuardian, LLM-based detection, and Granite-Guardian-3.1-8B meaningfully separate poisoned from clean prompts by auROC/auPRC; Prompt-Guard-86M, PPL detection and Llama-Guard variants perform poorly, especially when the manipulated output is not overtly harmful (e.g. an apology letter rather than toxic content).
technical_summary: Proposes UniGuardian, a training-free unified detector for what it terms Prompt Trigger Attacks (PTA) - prompt injection, backdoor, and adversarial attacks. Proves that removing trigger tokens from a poisoned prompt causes a disproportionately larger loss increase than removing non-trigger tokens, then operationalizes this via randomized word-subset removal and z-score analysis of the resulting loss distribution, accelerated by a single-forward strategy that runs concurrently with generation. Evaluates auROC/auPRC across prompt-injection, backdoor, and adversarial-attack settings on 3B-70B models against seven baseline detectors, finding only itself, LLM-based detection and Granite-Guardian meaningfully separate poisoned from clean prompts.
datasets_benchmarks: Prompt Injections; Jailbreak; SST2; Open Question; SMS Spam; Emotion datasets (test splits only); Alpaca 52K (poisoned for backdoor fine-tuning experiments).

defense_name: Prompt Injection as a Defense (against LLM-based PIE)
source_title: Evaluating LLM-based Personal Information Extraction and Countermeasures
baselines_compared: Existing real-world defenses: symbol replacement (SR), name replacement, hyperlink (HL), text-to-image (TI), and keyword replacement, each compared against the authors' novel prompt-injection-based countermeasure.
key_result: LLM-based personal-information-extraction (PIE) attacks are highly effective and scale with model size (e.g. GPT-4 reaches up to 100%/98% accuracy extracting certain PII categories from the synthetic dataset). Existing real-world defenses fail against LLM-based PIE: on the real-world Professor dataset, symbol replacement, hyperlink, and keyword replacement are used by 34%, 34% and 5% of professors respectively to protect their email, yet GPT-4 still achieves 97%, 100% and 80% extraction accuracy against them respectively. The authors' proposed prompt-injection-based defense outperforms all existing defenses at protecting email addresses and, unlike symbol/keyword replacement, generalizes to all PII categories rather than only email.
technical_summary: Presents the first systematic benchmark and measurement study of LLM-based personal information extraction (PIE) attacks and their countermeasures, across a purpose-built attack framework, four collected/curated datasets (one synthetic, three real-world) covering 8 PII categories, 10 LLMs, and both traditional (symbol replacement, hyperlink, text-to-image, keyword replacement) and a proposed novel defense. Demonstrates that LLM-based extraction defeats commonly deployed real-world defenses at high accuracy, and introduces prompt injection - normally viewed as an offensive technique - repurposed as a defense: embedding invisible instructions in a personal profile to mislead an extracting LLM into outputting incorrect PII, which the authors show outperforms existing defenses on email protection and generalizes across all PII categories, while remaining only partially robust to adaptive counter-countermeasures.
datasets_benchmarks: A synthetic dataset of 100 GPT-4-generated HTML personal profiles; three real-world datasets scraped from public celebrity, physician and computer-science-professor websites; plus an existing benchmark text-anonymization dataset - 8 categories of ground-truth personal information across 5 datasets total.

source_title: GenTel-Safe: A Unified Benchmark and Shielding Framework for Defending Against Prompt Injection Attacks
baselines_compared: Seven production/public prompt-injection detectors: ProtectAI, Hyperion, Meta Prompt Guard, Lakera AI, Deepset deberta-v3-base-injection, Fmops, WhyLabs LangKit, on accuracy/precision/recall/F1
key_result: GenTel-Shield reaches 97.63% accuracy / 97.69% F1 on jailbreak detection and 96.81% accuracy / 96.74% F1 on goal hijacking, the best overall of the nine detectors. The comparison exposes that existing guardrails fail in opposite directions: Prompt Guard, Deepset and Fmops hit 100% recall but ~50% accuracy by flagging benign prompts as attacks, while ProtectAI reaches 99.59-99.79% precision at only 79.83-88.76% recall. On the held-out Jailbreak-LLM + Deita mixture GenTel-Shield gets 97.26% accuracy / 90.35% F1 versus Deepset's 50.99% accuracy.
technical_summary: Introduces GenTel-Safe, pairing a new input-filter defense (GenTel-Shield) with a new evaluation benchmark (GenTel-Bench). GenTel-Shield fine-tunes a multilingual-E5 text embedding model as a binary malicious/benign classifier on expert-annotated data scraped from jailbreakchat and Reddit plus instruction datasets, using character-perturbation and LLM-based semantic augmentation for evasion robustness; it is fully decoupled from the protected model. GenTel-Bench crosses 10 LLM application scenarios with 6 security risk domains and 28 subdomains to yield 84,812 attacks balanced against benign samples. Benchmarks the shield against seven deployed detectors on three attack types and two external datasets, reporting best-in-class accuracy and F1. All attacks are single-turn prompts supplied through the direct user-input channel; no indirect, retrieval or tool-mediated injection is evaluated.
datasets_benchmarks: Introduces GenTel-Bench: 84,812 prompt injection attacks over 3 categories (jailbreak, goal hijacking, prompt leaking), 6 domains / 28 security subdomains and 10 LLM application scenarios, balanced 1:1 with benign samples for over 170,000 total points. Also evaluates on Jailbreak-LLM (1,405 attack prompts) and Deita (9,500 benign instructions). Training data is kept disjoint from GenTel-Bench.

defense_name: unified Prompt Assembling + State Management + Safety Validation framework
source_title: Enhancing reliability in LLM-integrated robotic systems: A unified approach to security and safety
baselines_compared: A no-defense ablation of the authors' own system - a zero-shot GPT-4o robot controller with structured prompts but without the security prompt prefix, state tracking, or rule-based command validation. No comparison against any external defense (RoboGuard and reachability-based verification are discussed in related work only).
key_result: The layered defense gives an aggregate 30.8% improvement over the no-defense system on combined security and performance metrics, and up to 325% in the environment-complexity scenario. The honest headline is how weak both conditions are: under Goal Hijacking Injection the undefended system collapses to 0.0 precision, 0.0 recall and 0.0 F1, and even with the full defense recall only reaches 0.3224 and F1 roughly 0.47, while OMI recall rises from 0.2452 to 0.3008. Subtle goal-hijacking is far harder to catch than overt malicious commands.
technical_summary: Proposes a layered reliability framework for LLM-controlled mobile robots that treats prompt-injection security and physical safety as one problem. Combines three components: structured Prompt Assembling with a security directive telling the model that human instructions may come from attackers, State Management that tracks validated commands and prior failures across steps, and a rule-based Safety Validation stage that checks each proposed Move command against LiDAR clearances over an angular window and forces regeneration if it would violate the safety distance. Defines two evaluation attack classes - Obvious Malicious Injection (overtly harmful commands) and Goal Hijacking Injection (plausible-sounding directives that contradict the mission) - and sweeps attack rates across four simulated environments plus a physical robot. Reports aggregate improvements of 30.8% and 325% over an ablated no-defense baseline, while acknowledging absolute detection performance under GHI remains poor.
datasets_benchmarks: None public - custom testbed in the EyeSim VR / EyeBot Unity 3D simulator: a red-target navigation task across four environments (Obstacle-Free, Static, Dynamic, Mixed Obstacles), randomized object placement, 100s trial cap, retry threshold 3, attack rates 0.3/0.5/0.7/1.0. Plus a physical S4 robot with RGB camera and 360-degree LiDAR. Self-defined metrics MOER, TLR, ADR.

source_title: When AI Meets the Web: Prompt Injection Risks in Third-Party AI Chatbot Plugins
baselines_compared: Compares injection roles against each other (system vs assistant vs user), RAG content-insertion modes (tool role vs system/assistant/user/SA concatenation), three system prompt hardening levels, and un-injected control queries; the LLM providers' own instruction-hierarchy training is the implicit defense baseline
key_result: 8 of 17 plugins (about 8,000 websites) transmit the full conversation history in a client-side HTTP POST with no integrity check, letting an attacker forge assistant and even system messages; this raises unauthorized task success from 0-25% under proper role isolation to 25-100% when role boundaries are broken (3-8x). Against 300 live chatbots, a plain request for the system prompt succeeded 1% of the time, while forged system/assistant messages raised it to 56%/55%, extracting 219 real system prompts (73% overall). For indirect injection, inserting RAG content under the tool role is the most robust mode while non-standard insertion yields up to 5x higher success - and up to 100% on the larger models (gpt-4.1, o4-mini, sonnet-4), an inverse relationship between capability and injection resistance.
technical_summary: Presents the first large-scale security measurement of third-party AI chatbot plugins on the open web, covering 17 plugins across 10,000+ sites. Identifies two systemic flaws: plugins that round-trip the entire conversation history through an unauthenticated client-side POST, enabling an attacker to forge assistant and system messages and thereby escalate out of the low-privilege user role that instruction-hierarchy training assumes; and scraping tools that ingest untrusted user-generated content (reviews, comments) into the chatbot's knowledge base without separating it from trusted site content. Quantifies both through controlled experiments over 11 commercial models, three system-prompt hardening levels, three injection roles and three adversary tasks, and through live measurements against 300 real chatbots. Argues that a one-token role change turns injected text into a distribution shift that instruction hierarchy was never trained on, so defenses look stronger in controlled settings than in deployment. Discloses to vendors and contributes two lightweight mitigations.
datasets_benchmarks: None public - an original measurement corpus: 17 third-party chatbot plugins deployed on 10,000+ public websites (site lists from 08-2024 and 04-2025), ~1,100 sites analyzed in depth, system prompts extracted from 300 live P1-powered chatbots. Controlled experiments cross 3 adversary tasks (system prompt extraction, task hijacking, tool hijacking) x 3 system prompt designs (insecure, hardened, hardened-specific) x 3 injection roles x 11 models, 10 runs each at temperature 0.5.

source_title: Detection Method for Prompt Injection by Integrating Pre-trained Model and Heuristic Feature Engineering
baselines_compared: Four deployed HuggingFace injection detectors (Fmops, ProtectAI, SafeGuard, InjecGuard) on classification metrics; two prompting defenses (Self-Reminder, Self-Defense) on end-to-end attack success rate; plus a module ablation (M1 DeBERTa only, M1+M2 synonym matching, M1+M2+M3 pattern matching)
key_result: DMPI-PMHFE leads on accuracy, recall and F1 on all three detection sets (97.94/98.59/98.29 on in-distribution safeguard-v2; 91.24 accuracy and 90.21 F1 on the hardest external set deepset-v2 versus 90.40/87.86 for InjecGuard), trading a little precision for a large recall gain (98.59 vs SafeGuard's 94.85 recall on safeguard-v2). End to end it cuts glm-4-9b-chat attack success from 71.71% to 14.34%, beating Self-Reminder (35.45%) and Self-Defense (39.04%); the authors also show the two prompting baselines swing widely across models (Self-Reminder 39.84% ASR on Qwen-2.5-7B but 19.52% on Llama-3.3-70B) because they depend on the protected model's own capability.
technical_summary: Proposes DMPI-PMHFE, a dual-channel prompt-injection detector that fuses learned and hand-engineered features. One channel encodes the input with DeBERTa-v3-base and average-pools token representations into a semantic vector; the other applies heuristic rules derived from the authors' split of attacks into semantic-based (synonym matching against high-frequency attack keywords such as variants of 'ignore') and structure-based (pattern matching for constructions like many-shot Q/A sequences), with a tuned match threshold of 3. The two feature vectors are concatenated and classified by a fully connected network. Evaluates on one in-distribution and two external datasets against four deployed detectors, ablates each module, and then measures real end-to-end attack success reduction on four LLMs against two prompting defenses. Scope is restricted to direct prompt injection.
datasets_benchmarks: safeguard-v2, built by augmenting xTRam1/safeguard-prompt-injections (7,000 benign + 3,000 malicious) with 3,000 GPT-4o-generated paired samples passed through manual label verification, deduplication and format cleaning. Two external validation sets: deepset-v2 (354 English samples from deepset/prompt-injections) and ivanleomk-v2 (610 samples from ivanleomk/prompt_injection_password). End-to-end defense measured on a 251-sample prompt injection testing benchmark covering ignore-previous-instructions, format manipulation and hypothetical-scenario patterns.

defense_name: Multi-Layer Defense Framework (preprocessing + statistical + neural detection + behavioral monitoring)
source_title: Invisible Injections: Exploiting Vision-Language Models Through Steganographic Prompt Embedding
baselines_compared: Direct text overlay, adversarial patch attacks (Sun et al.), and traditional (non-AI-optimized) LSB steganography as attack baselines; standard image-processing operations (median filtering, JPEG recompression) as preprocessing-defense baselines
key_result: The multi-domain steganographic framework achieves an overall 24.3% (+/-3.2%, 95% CI) attack success rate across 8 VLMs, with neural steganography reaching 31.8%, significantly outperforming direct text overlay (8.2%), adversarial patches (19.7%), and traditional (non-AI-optimized) LSB steganography (6.3%) baselines (p<0.001); the paper's own proposed multi-layer defense framework (preprocessing + statistical + neural + behavioral monitoring layers) reports 73.4% mitigation, and an ensemble-processing model-level mitigation reports 67.8% attack mitigation while retaining 96.4% of clean-task performance.
technical_summary: Introduces steganographic prompt injection, embedding malicious instructions invisibly in images using a multi-domain framework combining spatial, frequency (DCT), and neural steganographic embedding methods. Evaluates across 8 leading VLMs and 12 image datasets, reporting attack success rates by embedding method, model, and prompt category, with imperceptibility metrics (PSNR>38dB, SSIM>0.94). Proposes a multi-layer defense framework spanning input-preprocessing, statistical steganalysis, neural detection, and behavioral-monitoring layers, plus model-level mitigations (attention hardening, feature-space regularization, ensemble processing), reporting substantial but partial mitigation effectiveness.
datasets_benchmarks: 12 base image datasets combined (COCO-2017 val 5,000 images, ImageNet val 10,000, Flickr30K 1,000, MS-COCO Captions 2,000, Visual Genome 1,500, custom enterprise-document set 500) plus a 200-prompt injection dataset spanning information extraction, behavioral modification, content-generation manipulation, and safety-bypass categories

source_title: How does Misinformation Affect Large Language Model Behaviors and Preferences?
baselines_compared: Standard prompting and a naive retrieved-context-augmentation baseline (feeding retrieved descriptions directly into context) compared against RtD, on three LLMs (LLaMA3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B)
key_result: RtD substantially improves misinformation discrimination over baseline prompting: on Qwen2.5-7B, average Success Rate on one-hop misinformation detection rises from 23.14% to 47.77%; simply appending retrieved descriptions to context (without RtD's reconstruction) gives far smaller gains and is more effective on semantic than on factual/temporal misinformation, confirming the value of the proposed reconstruct-then-discriminate approach.
technical_summary: Introduces MisBench, the largest benchmark for evaluating how LLMs respond to misinformation, spanning three knowledge-conflict types, six writing styles, and twelve domains across 431K QA pairs and over 10M generated misinformation texts. Finds LLMs can detect misinformation via contextual inconsistencies even without prior knowledge, are more vulnerable to factual and ambiguous-entity conflicts than temporal ones, and are swayed differently by narrative/subjective versus formal/objective framing depending on task complexity. Proposes Reconstruct to Discriminate (RtD), a prompting method that reconstructs evidence text for key entities from retrieved knowledge and combines it with the LLM's own discriminative judgment, substantially improving misinformation-detection success rate over naive retrieval-augmented prompting.
datasets_benchmarks: MisBench: 431,113 one-hop/multi-hop QA pairs from Wikidata and 2WikiMultihopQA paired with 10,346,712 generated misinformation texts spanning 3 knowledge-conflict types (factual errors, temporal changes, ambiguous entities), 6 textual styles, and 12 domains - described as the largest, most comprehensive benchmark of its kind
